title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) in Login Form
description: The login endpoint at /login is vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. The application does not implement CSRF token validation or perform proper Origin/Referer header verification. An attacker can craft a malicious webpage that, when visited by a logged-in user, can perform login actions on their behalf without authentication. The login form lacks any CSRF protection mechanism - no anti-CSRF tokens are present in the HTML form.
impact: An attacker can perform account takeover attacks by tricking users into visiting malicious websites that submit login forms to the vulnerable application. This can lead to unauthorized access to user accounts. Additionally, this vulnerability can be chained with account enumeration to target specific users. An attacker could also use this to automate credential stuffing attacks or brute force attempts against the login endpoint without CSRF protection.
evidence:
POC execution confirmed the vulnerability:

1. Form Inspection: No CSRF token field found in login form - login form contains only username and password fields with no anti-CSRF token.

2. Cross-Origin Request Test: 
   - Command: curl -X POST -H "Origin: http://evil.com" -H "Referer: http://evil.com" -d "username=test&password=test" http://localhost:8080/login
   - Response: HTTP 302 redirect with Set-Cookie: session=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoxfQ.aS8SJQ.BQaYhF3t1RlXTDoqtCFnl7HzT8Q
   - Result: Login succeeds with cross-origin request from evil.com

3. Vulnerability Confirmed:
   - Application accepts login requests from different origins
   - No CSRF token validation performed
   - Origin/Referer headers not validated or enforced
   
POC output shows successful exploitation with session cookie being set despite cross-origin origin header indicating the request came from evil.com.
remediation:
1. Implement CSRF token generation and validation for all state-changing operations (POST, PUT, DELETE)
2. Add a hidden CSRF token field to the login form generated server-side with unique, non-predictable tokens
3. Validate the CSRF token on POST submission before processing the login
4. Implement SameSite cookie attribute on session cookies (SameSite=Strict for highest security, or SameSite=Lax as minimum)
5. Validate Origin and Referer headers to ensure requests originate from the application's domain
6. Use security-focused frameworks with built-in CSRF protection (e.g., Flask with Flask-WTF, Django CSRF middleware)
7. Consider implementing Double-Submit Cookie pattern as an alternative CSRF protection mechanism
8. Add Content Security Policy (CSP) headers to restrict form submissions to same-origin
references: OWASP Top 10 2021 - A01:2021 - Broken Access Control, CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
toolCallDescription: Document the CSRF vulnerability in login endpoint with confirmed POC demonstrating cross-origin request acceptance without token validation
